label: spatial postpositions: on, under, behind, in front of
note: Chapter 84. The old note was exact: 'the track teaches five house objects and no way to say where any of them is.' All four of the words it named are now taught -- mukalil, thaazhe, munnil, pinnil -- but the chapter's first lesson spends itself on the SHAPE rather than on vocabulary, because the shape is what makes each later place-word cost a word and nothing else. THE NOUN IN FRONT TAKES THE GENITIVE, and that is not new grammar: it is chapter 78's ending, unchanged, picking its form by the last sound of the noun. The reason is worth having -- kaseerayude mukalil is literally 'the chair's top-part', so Malayalam is not saying ON the chair but naming a part that BELONGS to it, which is exactly why the owner-ending is required to connect the two words at all. The recall lesson then states a pattern that covers THREE of the four: mukalil, munnil and pinnil visibly end in the locative -il, because they are part-words already sitting in the in-form, while thaazhe ends in -e and does not. That is stated plainly rather than tidied away, since a reader who notices the exception has read correctly. Verified before writing: all four returned ZERO files. MEESHA (table) was deliberately NOT taught even though the point's domain invites it: it already appears untaught in ML-C52-chair's etymology prose, so taking it as a headword would convert that use into a forward reference -- the ML-C82-chechi-address trap. The examples use kaseera, which is taught.
